assessment.nobel_worthiness: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice idea removes Doppler and recoil shifts while keeping many atoms, and Ye's strontium realization pushed clocks to roughly 1e-18 fractional uncertainty. It is a clean and somewhat unexpected route to extreme precision, enabling tests of fundamental constants, gravitational time dilation over millimetres, and a path to redefining the second. As an atomic theorist I value that the result is quantitative and understood from first principles.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the optical lattice clock concept and demonstrated early strontium operation; Ye's JILA group drove the performance frontier and the systematics and many-body understanding. A two-name prize is a fair configuration. The 2005 prize (Hall, Hänsch) honoured the frequency comb, so this is a distinct step.
assessment.maturity: Several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others) operate and compare lattice clocks, and the community is preparing a redefinition of the second. Mature and timely.
uncertainties: Contributions from other precision-clock work (for example ion clocks) and how much of it should be recognised alongside lattice clocks cannot be settled from the supplied text.
I rely on memory for exact accuracy figures and dates and have not verified them independently.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry makes the wave nature of matter into a precision sensor for gravity, rotation and constants, and into tests of the equivalence principle. It speaks directly to the quantum-classical boundary I find compelling and has real instrumentation consequences.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard's group pioneered atom optics and early interferometry with gratings; Kasevich (with Chu) made the light-pulse interferometer a precision gravimeter and gyroscope; Mlynek's group did early grating and double-slit atom experiments. Two names is defensible but leaves Mlynek out, and people outside the supplied list (Chu, Bordé) complicate a fair split.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many laboratories, with field instruments and large-baseline tests under way. The core science is mature, while the headline fundamental tests are still improving.
uncertainties: Allocation of credit among Pritchard, Kasevich and Mlynek is unresolved, and the roles of people outside the credited names matter.
Some of the most ambitious claims (large momentum transfer, long baselines) are still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cirac and Zoller proposed trapped-ion quantum gates and later quantum simulators, and Blatt realized high-fidelity gates and digital simulation with ions. The work shows that individual quantum systems can be controlled well enough to compute and simulate, a fundamental advance in how quantum mechanics is used.
assessment.attribution: The Cirac-Zoller 1995 proposal is the key theoretical idea and Blatt's group gave decisive implementations. Bloch fits more naturally with the optical-lattice simulation candidate. The boundary with the 2012 prize to Wineland needs careful handling.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced across ion and atom platforms and now a large field. The 2012 and 2022 prizes reduce the novelty available, so timing is less pressing.
uncertainties: Overlap with already recognised work on ion control and entanglement could make a new prize look redundant.
Whether theory and experiment credit fit one prize without Bloch is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect showed that potentials have physical consequences in quantum mechanics, and Berry's geometric phase revealed a general structure in adiabatic evolution that runs through molecules, atoms and topological matter. Few ideas are as unexpected and as widely used.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov carries the 1959 effect (Bohm is not among the credited names) and Berry is the central figure for the 1984 geometric phase. The two-name configuration is plausible but combines two related, distinct discoveries.
assessment.maturity: Both effects are confirmed in many experiments and are textbook material. The concern is timeliness and the compound nature of the claim, not confirmation.
uncertainties: The prize would join two separate discoveries, and contributions by people outside the supplied names (for example Bohm, Pancharatnam) are not represented.
Whether the age of the discoveries makes recognition now appropriate is a judgement call.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light beats the standard quantum limit in interferometry and is now used in gravitational-wave detectors. Caves identified the limit and the remedy, and experiments showed it works in kilometre-scale instruments.
assessment.attribution: Caves provided the theoretical proposal, Kimble contributed early squeezed-state generation and cavity QED, and Schnabel's group developed detector-grade squeezing at GEO600 and beyond. Mavalvala is a strong alternative. Early experimental squeezing (Slusher and colleagues) is outside the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: The method is proven in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600 operation. Recognition is plausible, but the 2017 prize already covered gravitational-wave detection.
uncertainties: Credit for the first experimental squeezing lies outside the supplied names and could challenge fairness.
Choosing among Schnabel, Mavalvala and Kimble is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution ties the foundations of quantum mechanics (no cloning, entanglement) to secure communication and was a conceptual starting point for quantum information science. The idea is original and general.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard (BB84) are the clear originators, and Ekert's 1991 entanglement-based protocol connects to Bell tests. Three names are compatible with a prize, though Ekert's relative role is debated.
assessment.maturity: Many experimental demonstrations exist, along with satellite and commercial systems. The 2022 prize on Bell tests covers part of the foundational ground.
uncertainties: It may be judged closer to information science than to a physics discovery.
Practical implementation security is a separate issue from the principle.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realize Hubbard models cleanly, with the superfluid-Mott transition, single-site-resolved microscopy and Fermi-Hubbard experiments. This gives unusual quantitative control of many-body quantum systems, close to my own interests.
assessment.attribution: Greiner's Mott-insulator experiment, Bloch's lattice and microscopy work, and Esslinger's Fermi-Hubbard experiments are all important. Zoller supplied the theory proposal and is not in my proposed set, so theory credit remains open.
assessment.maturity: Mature and reproduced by many groups, though the central open questions (for example the low-temperature Fermi-Hubbard phase diagram) are not settled.
uncertainties: Bloch and Zoller are credited in B010 as well, so recognition could be split or duplicated.
The payoff for real solid-state problems is still emerging.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Titanium-sapphire gain media and Kerr-lens mode-locking provided broadband femtosecond lasers that underlie frequency combs, high-harmonic generation and attosecond physics, which I know well. The original motivation was technological, so it ranks lower for me than discoveries about nature.
assessment.attribution: Moulton developed the Ti:sapphire laser medium and Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens mode-locking. Other members of that team are not among the supplied names, so the configuration is incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Universally adopted with enormous downstream impact. Recognition would be overdue rather than premature, but it is an enabling instrument more than a conceptual finding.
uncertainties: The committee may regard it as enabling technology rather than a discovery of nature.
Credit for Kerr-lens mode-locking involves people outside the supplied names, and I cannot verify the original experimental details.
